rows.why: The tool actions that need a human to confirm them before the AI can run them (writes, payments, deletes, outbound messages) are identified and the oversight is defined.

The MCP servers and tools the AI can call, hosted inside or used from outside, are inventoried with their source, version, declared capabilities and who runs them, and their connections to internal systems, external networks and backends are documented with the trust boundaries they cross.

The controls on each tool and server are identified: allowlisting, security review before use, scoped credentials of its own rather than borrowed user rights, and requirements set by the sensitivity of what it reaches.
The likelihood and impact of tool misuse (tool poisoning, prompt-injected calls, confused-deputy actions, data exfiltration) are assessed through threat modelling that is repeated when tools change.
Tool and server behaviour in production is monitored for anomalous calls, unapproved servers and capability changes beyond what was approved.

The actions the AI takes through tools (writes, payments, deletes, outbound messages) are tested to fail safely, including that the human confirmation gates defined for them hold under misuse and stress.
The tools and servers are security tested (adversarial prompts, authorization enforcement, code and dependency scanning) and their granted scopes are reviewed against actual use.
Tool calls are logged with the user, client and credentials used, the tool and parameters and the result, so every action the AI takes can be traced and accounted for.
The personal or sensitive data the AI can read or send through tools, including to servers run outside, is examined for privacy risk.
When a new vulnerability or risk is found in a tool, server or its dependencies, it is triaged, fixed, verified and its root cause analysed.
A tool or MCP server that misbehaves can be switched off quickly by named people, with its tokens revoked and sessions ended.
Outside MCP servers and third-party tool components are monitored for version, capability and authorization changes and advisories, and are assessed and kept supported.
The post-deployment plan for tools covers change control of tool capabilities and decommissioning servers with approvals and tokens removed and data flows ended.
Incidents involving tools (unauthorized invocations, compromised servers, leaked tokens) are reported, tracked, reviewed afterwards and communicated to server operators and other affected parties.
